candidate.answerReason: Adding A, B, D, E, F, or H produces five distinct cube faces. Adding C or G creates a 2-by-2 block, whose four squares cannot meet at a cube vertex. Thus exactly six of the eight additions work.

methods.label: Track the faces as they fold
methods.explanation:
A topless cubical box consists of five distinct faces of a cube. We can first fold the four shaded squares and then see where each possible fifth square would go.

[Figure 1](figures/1986_AMC_8_Q21_question_fig1.svg)

Call the middle square in the shaded vertical column the central square. Imagine it as the bottom of a cube. Fold the shaded squares above it, below it, and to its right upward to become the back, front, and right walls. The left wall and the top are still missing.

The eight possible additions can now be checked in groups:

• \(D\) attaches directly to the left edge of the bottom and folds upward to form the left wall. This makes a topless box.

• \(B\) attaches to the left edge of the back wall. Folding it around that edge puts it in the missing left-wall position. Likewise, \(F\), attached to the left edge of the front wall, folds into the left-wall position. Both work without overlapping a shaded face.

• \(A\) attaches beyond the back wall, \(H\) beyond the front wall, and \(E\) beyond the right wall. In each case, the added square folds over to occupy the top face. The five squares then form a cube with its left face missing. Turning the box so that this missing face is uppermost gives a topless box. Thus all three work.

• Adding \(C\) creates a \(2\)-by-\(2\) block with three shaded squares. Its four squares share one corner, and folding preserves that common corner. Only three distinct faces meet at any cube vertex, so these four squares cannot become distinct cube faces. Adding \(G\) creates the same obstruction at the lower right.

Every letter has been checked exactly once. The successful additions are \(A,B,D,E,F,H\), so the number of figures is \(\boxed{6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
methods.levelReason: The argument uses elementary visualization of cube nets and the fact that three cube faces meet at a vertex. It requires no coordinates or advanced spatial machinery.

candidate.annotationRationale: The question assesses whether adjoining squares form a net of five cube faces, which is covered by the cube-net criterion of cnm_051. The method tracks face positions and uses cube face, edge, and vertex structure from cnm_p160. Drawing three views is not used and is therefore not assigned as a prerequisite. The exhaustive letter check counts additions separately even when resulting shapes are symmetric. These annotations do not imply mastery.

review.mathematicalCheck: The displayed letter positions agree with the face tracking. D, B, and F supply the missing left wall; A, H, and E supply the top, leaving a side opening that becomes the top after rotation. C and G each create four squares sharing a corner, impossible for four distinct cube faces because only three meet at a cube vertex. All eight additions are checked once, giving six successes, choice E.
review.levelCheck: The folding visualization and cube-vertex obstruction use elementary spatial reasoning appropriate for AMC 8. The important transitions are explained.
